Thinking While Listening:
Fast–Slow Recurrence for Long-Horizon Sequential Modeling

Shota Takashiro Affiliation: The University of Tokyo, Hongo 7-3-1, Bunkyo-ku, Tokyo, 113-8656 Japan Correspondence to: takashiro@weblab.t.u-tokyo.ac.jp    Masanori Koyama Affiliation: The University of Tokyo, Hongo 7-3-1, Bunkyo-ku, Tokyo, 113-8656 Japan    Takeru Miyato Affiliation: University of Tübingen, Tübingen, Germany    Yusuke Iwasawa Affiliation: The University of Tokyo, Hongo 7-3-1, Bunkyo-ku, Tokyo, 113-8656 Japan    Yutaka Matsuo Affiliation: The University of Tokyo, Hongo 7-3-1, Bunkyo-ku, Tokyo, 113-8656 Japan    Kohei Hayashi Affiliation: The University of Tokyo, Hongo 7-3-1, Bunkyo-ku, Tokyo, 113-8656 Japan
Abstract

We extend the recent latent recurrent modeling to sequential input streams. By interleaving fast, recurrent latent updates with self-organizational ability between slow observation updates, our method facilitates the learning of stable internal structures that evolve alongside the input. This mechanism allows the model to maintain coherent and clustered representations over long horizons, improving out-of-distribution generalization in reinforcement learning and algorithmic tasks compared to sequential baselines such as LSTM, state space models, and Transformer variants.

Keywords: 
Machine Learning, ICML

1 Introduction

Humans are capable of reasoning while simultaneously processing external inputs, allowing them to cope with long-horizon streams of variable lengths (Baddeley, 1992; Hasson et al., 2015). In such settings, an agent must maintain and update an internal state that summarizes past information while processing new observations, selectively extracting task-relevant signals and retaining them until future inputs resolve their relevance. Such a state-tracking type computation is central to navigation, decision-making, and prediction in nonstationary environments (Kaelbling et al., 1998; Thrun, 2000; Hausknecht and Stone, 2015). However, learning to reliably maintain such an internal state over long horizons is a well-known challenge for recurrent neural networks (Bengio et al., 1994; Pascanu et al., 2013) and it remains a major bottleneck in modern neural sequential models such as Transformers (Tay et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2023; Sinha et al., 2025).

To explore this endeavor, we draw on recent advances in latent recurrent modeling (Geiping et al., 2025; Hao et al., 2024a; Gladstone et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025; Miyato et al., 2025; Darlow et al., 2025; Koishekenov et al., 2025). These methods iteratively apply a recurrent block in latent space to a fixed input, learning an internal evolution of the state whose repeated application leads to improved performance. While they are often motivated as a mechanism to scale the test-time compute, we particularly want to exploit its ability to iteratively refine and organize the information in the latent space. This ability is supported empirically by recent works like (Miyato et al., 2025; Darlow et al., 2025) as well as by theoretical results showing that recurrent modules can dynamically cluster information (Kuramoto, 1984; Geshkovski et al., 2024; Geshkovski et al., 2025). These results suggest latent recurrent models as a promising computational core for “tracking the evolving state of both real and abstract worlds” (Li and Janson, 2025). However, the approaches we introduced above lack an explicit mechanism to scalably integrate evolving external inputs into the dynamics of the internal representation. In direct applications of these approaches, the latent state is reinitialized at the beginning of each loop that processes incoming input, and prior computation is preserved by appending latent summaries to the external context.

The goal of this work is to explore the extension of the recent latent recurrent model to evolving sequential inputs, so that new observations can be continuously incorporated into the latent representation of fixed size. We achieve this by reformulating the latent recurrent system as a pair of coupled dynamical processes: a fast-evolving latent reasoning process and a slow-evolving observation process. We refer to this architecture as Fast Slow Recurrent Model(FSRM). More concretely, without resetting the latent state, we run a continuous latent recurrence that is conditioned on external observations, which evolve on a slower timescale.

We study this construction through benchmark tasks that fundamentally require (i) selective extraction of task-relevant signals from long streams of variable lengths without storing the full history (ii) long-horizon retention of selected contextual information. Our strategy enables continuous integration of new observations while preserving the benefits of recurrent latent computation. As an example that highlights these requirements, we particularly consider the next token prediction task on Dyck language (Schützenberger, 1963), which we will elaborate in 5.2. On Dyck-(30,5), our model maintains 90%90\% token accuracy up to length 10510^{5} after training only on lengths ≤40\leq 40, whereas the accuracy of the frontier LLMs prompted with the rule of Dyck language decays rapidly with length under the same evaluation protocol (Figure 1). We also compare our approach against various competitive baselines, including SSMs and Transformers, on other benchmarks including reinforcement learning tasks. Finally, we provide qualitative visualizations illustrating how our architectural design transforms incoming information in a structured and traceable manner.

2 Preliminary: Latent Recurrent Model

Our method is inspired by models that conduct reasoning in the latent space by iterating a recurrent block (Gladstone et al., 2025; Geiping et al., 2025; Miyato et al., 2025). Given a specified number of recurrent iterations TT at training time, this class of approaches takes an observation OO as input together with an initial noise tensor 𝐗0∈ℝK×D\mathbf{X}_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times D}, where KK is the number of latent tokens and DD is the model dimension. The model then iteratively updates the latent state 𝐗⁡(t)\mathbf{X}(t) by initializing 𝐗⁡(0)=𝐗0\mathbf{X}(0)=\mathbf{X}_{0} and applying

𝐗⁡(t+1)=R⁡(𝐗⁡(t),Encoder⁡(O))\displaystyle\mathbf{X}(t+1)=R\left(\mathbf{X}(t),\mathrm{Encoder}(O)\right) (1)

for t=0,1,…,T−1.t=0,1,\dots,T-1. This produces 𝐗⁡(T)\mathbf{X}(T), a latent conclusion of depth TT. We use Decoder⁡(𝐗⁡(T))\mathrm{Decoder}(\mathbf{X}(T)) for inference.

This system can be applied autoregressively; for example, one may set Decoder⁡(𝐗⁡(T))\mathrm{Decoder}(\mathbf{X}(T)) to serve as the next observation OO in a subsequent round of reasoning. When applied autoregressively at turn index ss, models in this family typically use the accumulated set of the latent tokens 𝐗s​(T)\mathbf{X}^{s}(T), or its decoded form, as contextual input, and reinitialize 𝐗s​(0)\mathbf{X}^{s}(0) at every turn (Gladstone et al., 2025; Hao et al., 2024a). A naive extension of this strategy to an evolving observation sequence OsO_{s} is to concatenate {𝐗s​(T)}s\{\mathbf{X}^{s}(T)\}_{s} with {Os}s\{O_{s}\}_{s} as context, which causes the context length to grow with increasing ss. This introduces one source of long-horizon failure, namely the difficulty associated with the use of excessively long contexts (Liu et al., 2023; Shojaee et al., 2025). In the next section, we extend the latent recurrent model more directly so that the reasoning proceeds continuously while listening to an evolving stream of observations.

3 Fast–Slow Coupling of Latent Recurrence with the Observational Process

Our goal is to explore a system that can continuously integrate the evolving external signals into the latent reasoning process. To this end, we modify latent recurrent reasoning by considering a coupled dynamical system in which the observational process and the reasoning process evolve on the same timeline but at different speeds. In our model, the reasoning process proceeds TT times faster than the observation process, so that TT also represents the number of latent reasoning iterations performed per observation.

Let tt denote the fast time scale, and let s=⌊t/T⌋s=\lfloor t/T\rfloor denote the slow time scale indexing the observations, with observations given by OsO_{s}. Let 𝐂⁡(t)∈ℝK×D\mathbf{C}(t)\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times D} denote the encoded observation process and 𝐗⁡(t)\mathbf{X}(t) denote the latent process of thought, operating in the same latent space as 𝐂⁡(t)\mathbf{C}(t). The discretized dynamics of our model are given by

{𝐂⁡(t)=Encoder⁡(Os)for ​s=⌊t/T⌋∈{0,…,S−1},𝐗⁡(t+1)=Π⁡(𝐗⁡(t)+γ​F​(𝐗⁡(t),𝐂⁡(t),θ))for ​t∈{0,…,S​T−1},\left\{\begin{aligned} \mathbf{C}(t)&=\mathrm{Encoder}(O_{s})\\ &\hskip 14.22636pt\text{for }s=\lfloor t/T\rfloor\in\{0,\dots,S-1\},\\[6.0pt] \mathbf{X}(t+1)&=\Pi\left(\mathbf{X}(t)+\gamma F\left(\mathbf{X}(t),\mathbf{C}(t);\theta\right)\right)\\ &\hskip 14.22636pt\text{for }t\in\{0,\dots,ST-1\},\end{aligned}\right. (2)

where FF is a neural network parameterized by θ\theta and shared across timesteps, γ>0\gamma>0 is the step size, and Π⁡(𝐱)=𝐱/‖𝐱‖\Pi(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{x}/\|\mathbf{x}\| is a normalization operator. When the observation sequence has length SS, the recurrent module performs a total of S​TST latent updates while receiving SS encoded observation signals. Importantly, this differs from standard latent recurrent reasoning in that the time axis of the observation process is aligned with that of the fast latent reasoning, whose state transitions persist over time.

The latent state is initialized as 𝐗⁡(0)∼𝒩⁡(0,I)\mathbf{X}(0)\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I) at the beginning of each episode and is never reset until the episode ends; instead, it continuously moves forward in time and integrates the slow evolution of 𝐂⁡(t)\mathbf{C}(t) into its dynamics, even when the observational process evolves independently of 𝐗⁡(t)\mathbf{X}(t). See Figure 2 for visualization of our scheme.

We train the parameters θ\theta and γ\gamma as well as the encoder and decoder for various tasks that use the sequential output of 𝐗⁡(t)\mathbf{X}(t) for inference. For the prediction task on the observation sequence, Os+1O_{s+1} is predicted by Decoder⁡(𝐗⁡(s​T))\mathrm{Decoder}(\mathbf{X}(sT)).

3.1 The Choice of FF

For the choice of FF in our experiment, we explored a mechanism related to the architecture with self-organization properties (Kuramoto, 1984; Geshkovski et al., 2025; Geshkovski et al., 2024). In particular, we used the approach of Miyato et al. (2025) with attention-type update as follows:

F​(𝐗,𝐂)i\displaystyle F(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{C})_{i} :=𝛀i​𝐱i+Proj𝐱i​(J​(𝐗,𝐂)i)\displaystyle:=\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{i}\mathbf{x}_{i}+\mathrm{Proj}_{\mathbf{x}_{i}}\Big(J(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{C})_{i}\Big) (3)

where 𝐱i\mathbf{x}_{i} is the ii-th latent token in 𝐗\mathbf{X}, Proj𝐱​(𝐯)=𝐯−(𝐯⊤​𝐱)​𝐱\mathrm{Proj}_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{v})=\mathbf{v}-(\mathbf{v}^{\top}\mathbf{x})\mathbf{x} is the projection of the vector onto the tangent of the unit sphere, 𝛀i\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{i} is an anti-symmetric matrix, and each 𝐱i​(t)\mathbf{x}_{i}(t) is normalized so that the latent tokens remain on the unit sphere for every tt. Following Miyato et al. (2025), our JJ is an attention-based function that mixes latent tokens {𝐱i}\{\mathbf{x}_{i}\} while integrating 𝐂\mathbf{C} in an additive manner. Please see Appendix A.1 for details. We also observe that a variant where JJ is implemented as a vanilla Transformer block works competitively as well, but the model based on Miyato et al. (2025) performed most stably (Appendix C.3).

Energy-like scalar

This model also provides a scalar quantity that is useful for tracing the behavior of the latent updates. The update can be interpreted as a dynamical system of interacting latent tokens evolving toward self-organization, and there exists a tractable, energy-like scalar that represents the degree of self-organization of the neuronal population (Kuramoto, 1984); see Appendix A.2. In the experimental section, we will demonstrate that our model learns to dynamically align the interpretable structural properties of the system with this energy state.

4 Related Work

Recent studies have given birth to many models that utilize recurrent mechanisms in the latent space. Unlike approaches based on chain-of-thought (Wei et al., 2022; Kojima et al., 2022), Geiping et al. (2025) argue that such latent recurrent approaches do not require specialized training data, can work with small context windows, and can capture types of reasoning that are not easily represented in the output space, such as words and symbols. Geiping et al. (2025), similar to Miyato et al. (2025), propose the framework of applying a recurrent module to a randomly initialized latent signal while injecting the conditional input. Du et al. (2022) formulates a relevant mechanism through energy minimization in EBMs, and Gladstone et al. (2025) provides transformer-based instantiations. Unlike our approach, when we apply these approaches to sequential inputs, these methods decode each output, and the conditional context grows in length with the sequence. The same applies to Zhu et al. (2025) and Fan et al. (2025) as well. Coconut (Hao et al., 2024b), on the other hand, does not decode the output and conducts all computation of the sequence in the latent space. However, this approach also makes the conditional context grow in the latent space. Our approach carries over the latent variable over sequences of any length. Contexts are compressed and organized into a latent variable of fixed size through recurrence.

As a recurrent method that conducts all computations in the latent space of fixed dimension, we shall mention Perceiver (Jaegle et al., 2021), which proposes an RNN-style latent update to incorporate sequential signals. While related to our approach, this approach is not equipped with a recurrent reasoning loop that proceeds faster than the observations. Adaptive Computation Time (Graves, 2017) is also closely related to our approach, as it separates the fast-loop RNN from the slow input dynamics. However, it does not apply a recurrent mechanism with a self-organization property like a transformer (Geshkovski et al., 2024), and the latent at the end of the fast loop is not directly carried over to the next loop. Instead, the initial latent of the next loop is produced by the ensemble of the trajectories in the previous fast loop. Universal Transformer (Dehghani et al., 2019) uses recurrent self-attention, but without input injection. (Schöne et al., 2025) is more related to our approach, except that they use SSM to model the fast process, and introduce another auxiliary variable in the fast process that is initialized at every loop.

We shall also mention HRM (Wang et al., 2025), which is inspired by biological findings (Murray et al., 2014; Huntenburg et al., 2018; Zeraati et al., 2023), as well as its extension, TRM (Jolicoeur-Martineau, 2025). These methods also introduce a system of coupled fast and slow dynamics. However, unlike our approach, these methods do not consider temporally varying input sequences, and their reasoning is conducted on a stationary input. Also, CTM (Darlow et al., 2025) applies fast recurrence in autoregressive time segments, and is capable of handling the temporally varying input sequences. CTM frames their architecture as a dynamical system of interacting neurons (latents). Unlike our approach, they explicitly define the synchronization strength between each pair of neurons that is integrated over time, and produce the output from the synchronization pattern itself as opposed to our direct readout from the latents.

5 Experiments

We conducted a series of experiments to assess our model’s ability to dynamically integrate sequential inputs into its recurrent process in support of correct inference. We selected tasks that fundamentally require the model to iteratively and selectively identify task-relevant information from an evolving input sequence, and to consolidate it by continuously integrating this information into the latent state.

We first present results on the egocentric maze and Dyck tasks, both of which provide supervision in the form of correct answers. In these settings, the model can retrospectively infer which parts of the input are irrelevant to the correct underlying structure of the data. We additionally consider more challenging reinforcement learning tasks on MiniGrid. In these online settings, the model cannot directly compute the correct regret or value signal from immediate rewards, and therefore must learn indirectly how to integrate episodic information as it explores the environment.

Hyperparameter

For the maze and Dyck tasks, we first identified a common set of training hyperparameters—specifically the number of epochs, batch size, and learning rate—for which validation performance converged across all baselines. After fixing these shared settings, we further tuned model-specific hyperparameters (e.g., learning rate and hidden dimensionality) independently for each baseline in order to maximize validation performance. For the MiniGrid experiments, we adopted the same hyperparameters for all baselines as in Smirnov and Gu (2025), while tuning the hyperparameters of our proposed method separately. Also see Appendix (Tables 2 and 3).

5.1 Egocentric Maze

The goal of this task is to infer the shortest path from the start to the end, while receiving a stream of egocentric observations from a navigator exploring the maze. In this task, the information corresponding to dead-end paths is naturally task-irrelevant. In order for the model to be able to generalize its inference capability to OOD mazes of large size, the model must learn to efficiently integrate the task-relevant information and iteratively consolidate its hypothesis about the shortest path.

More specifically, the model in this task is given a sequence of local, cropped 7×77\times 7 neighborhood images OsO_{s} corresponding to the egocentric observations of a navigator agent that explores the maze following the right-hand rule (the model has no control over the navigator). The navigator streams egocentric observations until the goal is reached. The decoded output of the model is a sequence of movements (up, down, left, right, pause) corresponding to the estimated shortest path. Depending on the geometry of the maze, the length of the observation sequence SS naturally varies across samples. As a supervisory signal to be compared against the decoded output, we provide the model, at the end of each episode, with the true shortest path for the maze, represented in the same format. We evaluate accuracy using a binary exact-match criterion on the entire predicted action sequence, after removing all pause tokens from both the prediction and the ground-truth shortest path.

Setup

The mazes are generated randomly. During training, they are of size 19×1919\times 19. We evaluate the model’s generalization on out-of-distribution (OOD) mazes of size 39×3939\times 39. Figure 3 shows examples of mazes for both the in-distribution (ID) and OOD settings. In the OOD setting, the observation sequence length SS tends to be naturally larger.

We evaluate seven models on the maze task: LSTM, Transformer (TF), Mamba-2 (Dao and Gu, 2024), looped TF (Fan et al., 2025), S5 (Smith et al., 2022), CTM (Darlow et al., 2025), and our model. Our dataset contains 45,000 training and 5,000 validation examples, in which training mazes are generated so that shortest‑path lengths are uniformly distributed. For the default setting, we set T=5T=5. Hyperparameters are tuned on the ID validation set and used unchanged for OOD evaluation. See Appendix B.2 for details. We report the mean ±\pm sd over three seeds.

Results

Our model significantly outperforms all baselines on the maze task. As shown in Figure 4, it achieves near-perfect accuracy on the 19×1919\times 19 (ID) mazes and, crucially, demonstrates strong generalization to unseen 39×3939\times 39 mazes with approximately 60%60\% accuracy. In contrast, the baseline models all fail to generalize.

Effect of fast-loop iterations

The number of fast inner-loop iterations (TT) controls how many recurrent updates occur between successive observations (Eq. 2). To investigate whether the model benefits from longer recurrence, we conducted experiments with varying values of TT while keeping all other components fixed. As shown in Table 1, OOD accuracy improves monotonically as TT increases, with gains saturating beyond T=8T=8.

Effect of weight sharing (recurrence) in the fast loop

Our fast module applies the same update rule repeatedly for TT inner steps, i.e., it is recurrent or weight-shared across fast iterations. To investigate the importance of this recurrent structure, we replaced it with an unrolled residual stack of TT distinct layers, while keeping the overall fast–slow interface unchanged. The results (Table 1) show that weight sharing is crucial for OOD generalization: with the same inner-loop budget (T=5T{=}5), the non-recurrent 5-layer stack reduces OOD accuracy from approximately 0.60.6 to approximately 0.50.5. Increasing depth without sharing does not recover this performance: a 10-layer unshared stack further degrades OOD accuracy to approximately 0.450.45, even after adjusting the learning rate. These results support our design choice of a recurrent fast module. Please also see C.1.

5.2 Dyck-(k,m)(k,m)

We also experimented with the symbolic generalization task on Dyck-(k,m)(k,m) (Hewitt et al., 2020), with kk bracket types and maximum depth mm. Dyck is a stack-related task that heavily requires long-range lookup as well as iterative consolidation of the current stack structure, and it is the task referred to in the introduction. We set m=5m=5 and k=30k=30.

Given a streaming input of brackets as “[{([((”, the goal is to sequentially predict the next bracket token that closes the most recent unclosed bracket. For example, when the input sequence up to s=4s=4 is “({[]”, the prediction at s=4s=4 should be “}”. When there is no bracket to close, the prediction should be “*”; also see Figure 5.

The streaming sequence of brackets is analogous to an ever-growing stack of jobs, where the depth at time ss corresponds to the number of remaining brackets to close. By design, this task requires the model to remember all unclosed brackets for as long as the sequence continues. For example, for sequences of the form “[()()()()⋯\cdots” in Figure 5, the model must remember the unclosed “[” as long as the sequence continues. See B.3 for more details.

Setup

For the ID dataset, we randomly generate Dyck-(30,5)(30,5) strings. For the OOD dataset, we define a sequence to be an nn-regular run if it has the following structure: (i) it begins with a random sequence of open brackets of random length, and (ii) it is followed by an infinite repetition of depth-nn openings and depth-nn closings. For example, “({[([[]](()){{}}…” is a 22-regular run, and the one in Figure 5 is a 11-regular run. We use 11-regular run for the OOD evaluation.

We trained the model on 10,000 random strings in an ID dataset of length ≤40\leq 40. For evaluation, the model sequentially predicts on 1,000 nn-regular runs of length up to 2,560. Accuracy is computed for the prediction of each bracket. We compare our model against LSTM, Transformer, and Mamba-2, which achieved relatively good performance in the maze experiments.

Since this task involves a hierarchical structure, we evaluate an extended variant of Eq. 2 with two fast processes. Specifically, for ℓ=0,1,2\ell=0,1,2, we set 𝐗(0)​(t)=𝐂​(t)\mathbf{X}^{(0)}(t)=\mathbf{C}(t) and

𝐗(ℓ)​(t+1)=Π⁡(𝐗(ℓ)​(t)+γ​F​(𝐗(ℓ)​(t),𝐗(ℓ−1)​(t)))\displaystyle\small\mathbf{X}^{(\ell)}(t+1)=\Pi\left(\mathbf{X}^{(\ell)}(t)+\gamma F\!\left(\mathbf{X}^{(\ell)}(t),\mathbf{X}^{(\ell-1)}(t)\right)\right)

Predictions are obtained by decoding the last layer’s output at each slow-time index ss. See Appendix B.3 for details.

Results

Figure 6 shows token-level accuracy against the sequence length for both ID and OOD settings. On ID data, all models except the vanilla Transformer extrapolate reasonably well across sequence lengths. In contrast, on the OOD patterns of 11-regular runs, all baselines eventually fall to the chance level (0.50.5) as the sequence length increases. This chance-level behavior corresponds to the cases of failing to predict the token that closes the first open bracket (colored red in Figure 5). Our model, however, maintains near 100%100\% accuracy over indefinitely long sequences, indicating that it retains the information of the first opening token while correctly predicting all other subsequent closures.

Comparison to LLMs

To relate this benchmark to current foundation models, we also compared our model against three frontier LLMs on the same Dyck-(30,5)(30,5) task (see Figure 1 in the introduction). For the evaluation of our method in this comparative study, we used the model trained with the seed that attained the highest OOD accuracy at length 2,560 in producing Figure 6. In contrast to our model, which is trained only on raw Dyck strings of length ≤40\leq 40, the LLMs are provided with a natural-language prompt describing the ground-truth algorithm that generates the sequence and are instructed to iteratively execute it; see B.3 for more details of the setup. Despite their advantage in parameter scale and access to the explicit algorithm, their token-wise accuracy deteriorates as sequence length increases, whereas our model maintains accuracy above 90%90\% on sequences that are two orders of magnitude longer.

Emergent structure in layerwise energies and latents

Interestingly, through learning the prediction task, our model discovers latent reasoning that aligns with the structural organization of the Dyck language. Recall that for the recurrence used in our experiments (Section 3.1), there exists an energy-like scalar that reflects the organizational level of the state. We show the evolution of this energy in Figure 6, and the evolution of the latent in Figure 7. The energy of X(1)X^{(1)} spikes upon the arrival of a new token and then stabilizes at a level that depends on the bracket type and whether the current token is opening or closing. In contrast, the energy of X(2)X^{(2)} is largely insensitive to bracket identity and is instead organized by stack depth. This qualitative shift in energy organization indicates that the second fast process abstracts away from token identity and operates at a higher structural level. PCA projections of the latents for both X(1)X^{(1)} and X(2)X^{(2)} support this interpretation: the state trajectories form a crisp, spring-shaped manifold indexed by stack depth that remains coherent over long horizons. This structured organization in the learned latent space is similar to the report in (Zhu et al., 2025) that the looped model tends to produce interpretable reasoning traces. This behavior stands in stark contrast to Mamba (Figure 7(c)).

5.3 Reinforcement Learning

We next evaluate our model on challenging partially observable reinforcement learning tasks from the MiniGrid environment (Chevalier-Boisvert et al., 2023). We consider three MiniGrid tasks: DoorKey, MultiRoom, and LavaCrossing (see Figure 14). In these navigation tasks, DoorKey requires the agent to pick up a key, open a door, and then reach the goal in this order. MultiRoom requires the agent to open multiple doors sequentially to reach the goal. LavaCrossing requires the agent to reach the goal while avoiding the lava. In all tasks, the reward is provided only at the end of a successful episode (i.e., sparse rewards).

Most importantly, because these tasks do not provide a ground-truth supervisory sequence of actions, it is more difficult for the model to retrospectively infer which information in the episode is worth incorporating into its reasoning and consolidating into intermediate conclusions.

At each slow step, the agent receives an egocentric 7×77\times 7 observation with object/color/door-state channels. The agent then selects an action from the set as∈{left,right,forward,toggle,pickup,drop,done}a_{s}\in\{\texttt{left},\allowbreak\texttt{right},\allowbreak\texttt{forward},\allowbreak\texttt{toggle},\allowbreak\texttt{pickup},\allowbreak\texttt{drop},\allowbreak\texttt{done}\}.

Setup

We designed our evaluation protocol to test the model’s generalization capabilities in a zero-shot transfer setting. The agent is trained exclusively on the simplest ID configuration and is subsequently evaluated, without any further training, on more complex and previously unseen OOD environments, which are typically larger than the ID environments (see Table 4 in the Appendix for details). We compare our model against a few competitive sequence-modeling baselines, including LSTM, Mamba-2, and Transformer-XL. Results are averaged over five random seeds, and we report the mean and standard deviation.

All models are trained end-to-end using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO; Schulman et al. (2017)). For our model, the agent’s encoder (sensory module) first processes the input observations through a series of convolutional layers, followed by our recurrent core (Eq. 2). Please see Appendix B.4 for more details.

Results

Figure 8 shows the success rates across all MiniGrid tasks. Our model performs comparably to or better than the baselines across all tested environments. This suggests that the recurrent mechanism of thinking while listening is effective in these complex sequential decision-making problems as well. Also, we again observe a clear emergent structure in the latent space of our learned model. We find that fluctuations in the energy value reflect the agent’s level of “frustration”, for example, when the agent’s vision changes beyond a certain threshold (Figure 9). Figure 10 shows PCA-projected latent state transitions for DoorKey; irrespective of the trajectories, the model organizes its representations around key-events such as the “key pickup”, “door opening”, and “goal discovery.”

6 Conclusion

We proposed a recurrent model that integrates sequential observations into recurrent modeling. Across the tasks that require long horizon information of task-relevant information while tending to incoming observation of varying relevance, our approach consistently outperformed strong baselines, including an LSTM, Mamba-2, and Transformer-XL, and it demonstrated competitive generalization and decision-making in dynamic environments. This suggests the coupling of fast recurrent latent dynamics with slowly evolving observation dynamics as a promising mechanism for sequential inference over long-horizon.

Limitations and future work

Despite strong performance on controlled benchmarks, our study has several limitations. First, experiments are limited to relatively small-scale synthetic and grid-based domains, and we have not yet validated the approach on larger real-world tasks such as language, video, or robotics. Second, the proposed fast-slow architecture incurs computational overhead due to its double-loop structure, resulting in lower GPU efficiency and slower inference than standard baselines (Appendix, Figure 17); improving efficiency via recursion-friendly parallelization methods (e.g., (Danieli et al., 2025)) is an important future direction. Finally, we do note that there is a sensitivity to the random initialization, as observed in Figure 8. This suggests gradient instability from repeated layer reuse, as observed in RNNs (Pascanu et al., 2013), and motivates further architectural and optimization improvements.

Appendix A Model Details

A.1 Implementation of JJ

In our fast update rule (Eq. (3)), the interaction term JJ determines how latent tokens mix with one another while incorporating the encoded observation signal. We build on the attention-based design originally introduced in Miyato et al. (2025). The original implementation uses only attention as its core. We extend their JJ to an attention + MLP block: we first compute an attention update over the latent tokens (with the observation stream integrated additively), and then apply a position-wise MLP to the resulting features. The MLP uses a ReLU activation. We found that this simple extension yields a performance improvement on the maze task in particular. We use this implementation of JJ for all tasks reported in the paper. For the attention module, we use GTA (Miyato et al., 2023) as positional embeddings. Pseudocode is provided in Figure 11.

A.2 Energy-like Scalar

A key advantage of using the AKOrN model (Miyato et al., 2025) is its interpretation as an energy-based model. We define the scalar energy of the dynamics as

ℰ(𝐗)=−12∑i𝐱iTJ(𝐗,𝐂)i.\displaystyle\mathcal{E}(\mathbf{X})=-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i}\mathbf{x}_{i}^{T}J(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{C})_{i}. (4)

Under certain structural constraints on JJ, this value becomes a proper energy; the dynamics in Eq.3 always update the vectors in the direction that decreases Eq.4 (see Appendix A of  Miyato et al. (2025) for details). This energy is related to the one introduced in (Kuramoto, 1984), which represents the level of the organization of the set of token neurons. Moreover, the original paper shows that even without such constraints, the energy value aligns with the confidence of the model’s output. We also observe that the evolution of this energy value effectively summarizes the model’s dynamics across different domains/tasks, which we describe in detail in Section 5. Similar energy also exists for self-attention under a structural constraint (Geshkovski et al., 2025).

Appendix B Experiment Details

B.1 Hyperparameters

We report the main hyperparameters in Tables 2 and 3. For our model we only finetuned the rotation dimension and TT, which are specific to our model. rotation dimension was set to 22, and TT was set to 10.

B.2 Ego-centric Maze

Because the maze task is particularly related to memorizing task-relevant information, we experimented with a memory-inspired design of JJ. In particular, we wrapped the original attention-based JJ in Appendix A.1 with a GRU. Letting 𝐙t\mathbf{Z}_{t} denote the hidden state of the GRU, we replaced the original JJ with

JGRU​(𝐗,𝐂)=GRU​(J⁡(𝐗,𝐂),𝐙)i.\displaystyle J_{\mathrm{GRU}}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{C})=\mathrm{GRU}(J(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{C});\mathbf{Z})_{i}. (5)

where 𝐙\mathbf{Z} is updated at every fast step by the GRU’s internal recurrence (omitted for brevity). This module also acts as an internal filter of the interaction features, encouraging continuity of the effective coupling even when 𝐂t\mathbf{C}_{t} varies rapidly.

As shown in Figure 12, this design indeed improves performance. At the same time, note that our model outperforms the baselines on OOD with and without the GRU design. This suggests that the recurrent module itself is more essential to latent reasoning with evolving sequential input in a setting like the maze. This memory-inspired design was used only for maze experiments.

B.3 Dyck Language

The pseudocode of the two-stage architecture used for the Dyck language experiments is shown in Figure 13. We set the history size as H=4H=4. Hewitt et al. (2020) originally formulated this task as standard next-token prediction. However, because there are multiple valid choices for the type of the next open bracket, the task is not deterministic when formulated as pure next-token prediction. To eliminate this source of indeterminacy in accuracy evaluation, we restrict the predictor to output only the closing bracket.

For the comparison with production LLMs on Dyck-(30,5), we queried each model via its public API using a common prompt that describes the stack‑based algorithm (Table 7). Following Chae et al. (2024), we designed the prompt so that it clearly separates (i) a natural‑language specification of the ground‑truth stack algorithm from (ii) explicit execution instructions that tell the model to simulate this algorithm step‑by‑step and output only the prediction string. No additional fine‑tuning was performed; all models were evaluated in a pure inference setting. We set the temperature to 0 if the API accepts it, so that the model’s behavior is more deterministic.

Modern LLMs can adapt their test‑time compute by varying the length of their internal “reasoning tokens”, but commercial APIs strictly enforce a maximum on the total number of output tokens (reasoning plus final answer). As of November 2025, the documented upper limits for our models are 32k tokens for Claude Opus 4.5 and 64k tokens for both Gemini 3.0 Pro and GPT‑5.1. For each provider, we first empirically determined the longest Dyck input length for which the prompt, the model’s reasoning tokens, and the final prediction string all remain within this limit. We then generated 100 Dyck sequences at this length and measured token‑level prediction accuracy. Use of external tools such as Python interpreters or code execution APIs was explicitly disabled so that each model had to execute the algorithm internally.

For our proposed recurrent model, we used the same two‑layer Dyck architecture as in the main experiment (Section 5.2) and selected the checkpoint that achieved the best accuracy at the maximum length of 2,560. No additional training or hyperparameter tuning was performed when extending the evaluation to longer sequences. For reference, Table 8 shows an example of the internal reasoning tokens produced by Claude Opus 4.5 on a representative input.

B.4 Reinforcement Learning

In these tasks, the agents are required to navigate an environment to reach the goal, while:

  • •

    DoorKey: finding a key and unlocking a door

  • •

    LavaCrossing: avoiding the impassable lava river

  • •

    MultiRoom: going through multiple rooms with doors.

We provide the illustrated examples of the environment for each environment in figure 14. For the training of our model, we followed the strategy of Geiping et al. (2025); Wang et al. (2025) for computational efficiency and used the gradient truncation. In particular, we set T=10T=10, and backpropagated through only the last 55 iterations of the recurrent loop at each ss.

Appendix C Additional Results

C.1 Ablation on the recurrence (weight-shared structure)

We evaluated whether the recurrent (weight-shared) architecture is a factor underlying the performance improvements. We evaluate three models under the maze setup (Section 5.1):

  • •

    Recurrent (T=5T{=}5). Iterating the AKOrN update TT times with shared weights.

  • •

    Non-recurrent (T=5T{=}5). A stack of 55 distinct layers (no weight sharing), analogous to a standard deep residual stack.

  • •

    Non-recurrent (T=10T{=}10). A deeper stack of 1010 distinct layers.

All other components and training details follow our maze protocol.

For non-recurrent baselines, we scale the learning rate with depth as lr​(T)=Tbase/T×10−3\text{lr}(T)=\sqrt{T_{\text{base}}/T}\times 10^{-3}, Tbase=5T_{\text{base}}=5, according to the Depth μ\muP scaling rule (Yang et al., 2023). We found that without this scaling the accuracies dropped significantly in non-recurrent models.

Results

Table 6 reports mean ±\pm std over three seeds for validation ID (19×1919{\times}19) and OOD (39×3939{\times}39) mazes. Without weight sharing, increasing the number of layers from 55 to 1010 degrades OOD performance (from 0.5090.509 to 0.4450.445). This trend contrasts with the recurrent model, where increasing the number of inner-loop steps TT improves OOD accuracy. Increasing depth without sharing degrades OOD generalization, whereas increasing the number of recurrent updates TT in the shared model improves it. Simply stacking more independent layers does not reproduce the same benefits of a recurrent, weight-shared model.

C.2 Effect of Test-Time Scaling of Fast-Process Iterations TT

In Table 1 we showed how changing the number of fast inner-loop iterations TT during training affects performance. Here we ask the complementary question: keeping the learned weights fixed, what happens if we change TT only at inference time? We show the result of this test-time scaling in Figure 15 when TT was set to 1010 during training. Using a larger TT does not significantly harm the performance. Note that because we are aligning the time axis of the loop with that of the observation process, we are not using the loop in the same setting as (Geiping et al., 2025). It is possible that a careful balance of the fast and slow processes is important in pursuing scaling of TT at test time, and it is an important direction for future work.

C.3 Ablation on the Fast Module FF

In the proposed architecture, the fast module FF in Eq.2 is instantiated with an AKOrN layer, but in principle any recurrent block could be used in place of (3). To investigate this design choice, we performed an ablation study on the maze task by replacing FF with alternative modules. Specifically, we compared:

  1. 1.

    the original AKOrN fast module,

  2. 2.

    a Transformer block followed by an RMSnorm as a post-normalization, and

  3. 3.

    a standard LSTM cell.

In all cases, we used the same setup as in Section 5.1, and only changed the implementation of FF.

Results

Figure 16 shows the resulting ID and OOD accuracies. As we can see, using a transformer block for the recurrent module works competitively, although the model based on AKOrN shows the best performance. Meanwhile, LSTM does not perform as well as the other two, suggesting that the role of the self-organizing mechanism, like the ones studied in (Geshkovski et al., 2024; Kuramoto, 1984), is crucial.

C.4 Inference cost

Unlike SSMs and LSTMs, our proposed model performs TT forward passes for each observation. To quantify the resulting inference speed, we measured wall-clock time on the MiniGrid RL task. All models were implemented in PyTorch without using optimizations such as torch.compile, and timing was recorded on a single NVIDIA GH200 core. The results are shown in Figure 17. With the default choice T=5T=5, our method is roughly three times slower than the Mamba and Transformer baselines. We note that this computational overhead is partly due to software constraints: competing models rely on highly optimized CUDA kernels and mature library implementations, whereas our current implementation lacks comparable low-level optimizations. We therefore expect that specialized kernels and recursion-friendly parallelization strategies could substantially reduce this gap without changing the model architecture.

C.5 Parameter size vs OOD performance

As summarized in Table 3, our proposed model is roughly an order of magnitude smaller in parameter count than common sequence models. This is because the recurrent core is highly parameter-efficient, and because our implementation does not yet benefit from the kernel-level optimizations available for architectures such as LSTMs or SSMs; scaling up the model size would therefore lead to comparatively higher computational cost despite the smaller parameter count. A natural concern is therefore whether the observed generalization gains could be attributed to reduced overfitting due to the smaller model size.

We scale the channel width of our model to {64, 128, 256} and train on the maze task using the same data and protocol. Unless otherwise noted, all training hyperparameters follow Section 5.1 (see Appendix B.1). For this ablation, we set the batch size to 128128 and adopt a width-scaling learning rate lr=64/channels×10−3\text{lr}=\sqrt{64/\text{channels}}\times 10^{-3}.

Results

Table 5 reports OOD accuracy (mean ±\pm std over 3 seeds). The 256256-channel variant attains the best OOD performance, suggesting that increasing capacity does not necessarily lead to overfitting in this setting. These results indicate that our OOD gains cannot be explained solely by a smaller model size.
